all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: prototype
concepts.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.
Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

concepts.name: error prevention
concepts.definition: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

defining_facts.text: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

In system design, user errors cannot be completely eliminated, so a design should aim to keep error rates low; for example, close and start options for the same interface should not be placed side by side because a user may accidentally choose the wrong action.

Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

concepts.name: horizontal prototype
concepts.definition: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

defining_facts.text: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.

Horizontal prototypes are suitable for discussing, brainstorming, and eliciting user feedback about the look, feel, and appearance of an interface, including whether its appearance is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

concepts.name: vertical prototype
concepts.definition: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

defining_facts.text: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.
Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.

In the description of a vertical prototype, the term implemented and the term screen are generic, so implemented does not necessarily mean writing code, and screen can refer to a two-dimensional (2D) computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment.

In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

concepts.name: low-fidelity prototype
concepts.definition: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

defining_facts.text: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

concepts.name: storyboard
concepts.definition: To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

defining_facts.text: To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.

A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

never_defined.name: graphical user interface
never_defined.definition: Most standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces (GUIs) that allow developers to create applications or experiences without coding, so users with basic personal computer (PC) skills and non-programmers can learn and use them.

never_defined.name: interactive system
never_defined.definition: Extended reality systems belong to the broad class of systems called interactive systems.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

never_defined.name: system design
never_defined.definition: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

never_defined.name: low-fidelity cardboard mockup
never_defined.definition: Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost, and throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

never_defined.name: paper sketch
never_defined.definition: Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost, and throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

never_defined.name: module
never_defined.definition: Incremental prototypes are created when the system design divides the system into units or modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system.

never_defined.name: robust evaluation technique
never_defined.definition: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

never_defined.name: usability test
never_defined.definition: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

never_defined.name: domain expert
never_defined.definition: Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.

never_defined.name: usability issue
never_defined.definition: In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

never_defined.name: usability inspection
never_defined.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

never_defined.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

never_defined.name: low-fidelity vertical prototype
never_defined.definition: A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.

never_defined.name: scenario
never_defined.definition: In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.

never_defined.name: usability question
never_defined.definition: Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.

never_defined.name: report
never_defined.definition: For each usability question, evaluators must give a detailed report rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why.

never_defined.name: evaluation session
never_defined.definition: The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues.

never_defined.name: checklist
never_defined.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.
